newsitem.title: JAPAN: Rising Japan car exports spark US trade row fears.
newsitem.headline: Rising Japan car exports spark US trade row fears.

text.p: Japan's top carmakers boosted their exports in the last business year on the weak yen and robust U.S. demand for sport utility vehicles, but analysts said on Monday the news could spark fears of another bitter trade row with the United States.
Japan's top carmaker Toyota Motor Corp said its exports increased 12.4 percent to 1.31 million units in the year to end-March.
The nation's second-ranked carmaker Nissan Motor Co Ltd said its exports grew 0.8 percent to 598,244 units.
Exports at Honda Motor Co Ltd and Mazda Motor Corp grew by 6.7 percent and 8.6 percent respectively in 1996/97.
In March alone, Honda recorded the strongest growth among the top five carmakers. It saw a 50.6 percent year-on-year jump thanks to strong sales of its sport utility vehicle, the CR-V.
Honda said it expects its car exports to the United States to grow further this calendar year. It saw a 58 percent jump in its exports to the United States to 240,000 units in 1997.
Analysts said that the yen's retreat against the dollar boosted Japanese automakers' international price competitiveness, pushing up exports.
"The robust sales of sport utility vehicles in the North American market was a significant factor in the rise in exports," said Nobuaki Yanachi, senior analyst at Kankaku Research Institute Inc.
U.S. trade officials have already expressed concern about rising Japanese car exports and called for action to further open up Japan's markets to U.S. car products.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said last Friday that she was worried by recent trade trends, particularly a surge in Japanese car imports in the U.S. market during the first three months of this year.

"We don't want to see a significant increase in the Japanese trade surplus," she said. "The overall imbalance in U.S.-Japan auto trade and the first quarter surge in Japanese imports requires that we watch this situation closely."
Analysts said that trade friction between the Japanese and U.S. car makers could intensify, as the current growth in the North American auto market was likely to peak soon.

Japanese car makers enjoyed robust sales and increased output in the last financial year thanks to a sharp rise in demand ahead of an increase in the sales tax to five percent from three percent on April 1.

Toyota's domestic production in 1996/97 was up 10.3 percent to 3.50 million, while Nissan' output totaled 1.66 million, down 0.8 percent from a year ago. Honda's domestic car output rose 20.6 percent year-on-year to 1.15 million in 1996/97, while Mazda's output increased 1.4 percent to 781,363.
